vignette:
She shows up for our sessions directly from work, still wearing her transit uniform-navy blue slacks, a gray button-down, the little badge with her employee number. She's twenty-five, single, lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment with a fire escape she never uses. The first thing I notice is how she sits: always facing the door, hands on her knees, ready to move.

She doesn't start with the military. She starts with the bus. Every day she drives the 47 line through the east side of the city-past the strip malls, the hospital, the low bridge that always makes her flinch. She tells me about a passenger last week, a man in his fifties wearing a ball cap, who raised his voice at her when the bus was late. "His hand came up," she says, her voice flat. "Just to point at the schedule. But for a second, I saw it-I saw a hand holding a weapon, coming toward me." She locked the doors, refused to let anyone off or on for ten minutes. Dispatch had to talk her down over the radio.

The trauma happened when she was twenty-one, a specialist in the Army, deployed to a FOB in eastern Afghanistan. She doesn't talk about the firefight itself unless I ask directly, and even then she gives me the facts like she's reading from a report: improvised explosive device hit their convoy, the vehicle ahead of hers took the blast, she was the one who pulled the driver from the burning Humvee. The driver's name was Reyes. She still remembers the heat on her face, the smell of diesel and flesh, the way Reyes's left leg was gone below the knee. She didn't cry then. She doesn't cry now.

But she does other things. She sleeps three hours a night, maybe four, always with the bedroom door open so she can see the front door. She stopped drinking coffee because it makes her heart race and then the dread starts-the certainty that something terrible is about to happen, that she will have to react, that she will fail. She avoids the subway. She avoids crowds. She avoids men in uniforms, especially anyone wearing a ball cap or carrying a backpack too loosely.

On the bus, she has a system. She scans every face as they board, cataloging hands, posture, eye contact. If a passenger seems agitated, she'll skip their stop, drive past and let them off somewhere else. She has a mental map of all the hospitals along her route, all the police stations, all the places she could pull over and call for backup. She carries a personal alarm in her pocket, even though the bus already has a silent panic button. She tests the button twice a day.

Her social life is almost nonexistent. She used to have friends from her unit, but she stopped returning texts. They know what happened, she says. "They get it. But they also don't want to talk about it, and I can't talk about anything else." Her last date-nine months ago-ended when the man reached for her hand across the table and she knocked a plate off the table and ran to the bathroom. She still has nightmares about Reyes. In the dreams, his leg is still attached but he's on fire, and she can't reach him because the road keeps stretching.

She tells me she is not broken. She says this often, as if reminding herself. She drives her route. She pays her bills. She gets up every morning. But the terror is constant, a low hum in her chest that spikes unpredictably-a backfire, a car door slamming, a child yelling too close. When it spikes, she dissociates. She describes a feeling of watching herself from above, driving the bus, her hands moving on the wheel, her mouth saying "next stop," but she is not inside her own body. Those moments last minutes. She says she probably misses a few stops, but no one has complained.

In our sessions, she keeps her coat on. She checks the door every few minutes. She smiles in a way that doesn't reach her eyes. She is always ready to leave.
